newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: IFP INDECISION KEEPS S.AFRICA CONSTITUTION ON TRACK.
newsitem.headline: IFP INDECISION KEEPS S.AFRICA CONSTITUTION ON TRACK.

text.p: South Africa's hopes of starting the new year with a final apartheid-free constitution improved on Sunday when President Nelson Mandela's rivals refrained from demanding a major re-write.

Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi said his Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), which boycotted constitution-writing over the last 18 months, wanted informal talks on the subject with the African National Congress (ANC).

"It is in the interests of the country that we have a meeting with the ruling party," he told a news conference in Ulundi in his home province, KwaZulu-Natal, at the end of a two-day summit of IFP leaders.
They met to decide whether to rejoin the formal talks on the new constitution after the country's highest court rejected an earlier draft, written without the IFP and approved by parliament in May.
But the IFP took no final decision on rejoining the Constitutional Assembly, and time is running out.

A new version has to be submitted to the Constitutional Court by October 11 if it is to come into force in January to replace an interim constitution that was agreed during the dying days of the old apartheid regime.
The IFP's failure to make up its mind this weekend increases the chances that the law will be fine-tuned by the other parties and sent back to the court on time.

ANC leaders have said they are not willing to let the IFP reopen full negotiations over all aspects of the law as this could seriously delay its approval. The court also said it expected just minor amendments.
Buthelezi said that was one reason for his reluctance to get involved again.
His party boycotted the constitution-writing process when international mediation promised by the ANC over the parties' differences failed to materialise.
The nationally strong ANC wanted a powerful central government, the regional-based IFP wanted more powers for the provinces.
The Court rejected several parts of the draft law including the section on provincial powers which it said would be unacceptably weakened.
But it also threw out the IFP-shaped KwaZulu-Natal provincial constitution for the opposite reason, saying it usurped central powers as if it was a separate state.
IFP and ANC supporters have waged a low-level civil war for control in KwaZulu-Natal for a decade, but the fighting has died down since local elections in June.
Buthelezi said the rejection of his province's constitution could stir the conflict up again.
"There is a lot of anxiety amongst our members that the constitution agreed to by all KwaZulu-Natal parties being thrown out will promote that state of ungovernability," he said.
Political analysts said the IFP's weekend indecision showed it was internally divided and in a weak position.
